question_hint: On the fraud model resume, you say you chose class weights over resampling after an ablation. Take me through that ablation—what variants did you compare and what measurement made class weights win?
expected_points: Set up the same TimeSeriesSplit folds for every variant so comparisons were apples-to-apples.
Compared XGBoost class weights, random undersampling, and SMOTE; judged on the PR curve and recall at the target operating precision, not just AUC.
Class weights gave the best recall-at-90%-precision (0.62 vs. the alternatives) and kept the training/serving pipeline simpler.
Noted that resampling variants were sensitive to the resampling ratio and added complexity for no gain on the out-of-time validation set.
Re-checked the choice when class priors drifted in production, since the original ablation captured just one historical imbalance.

topic: Threshold tuning and business cost tradeoff
question_hint: You tuned to recall 0.62 at 90% precision. Where did the 90% precision number come from, and how did you make sure that threshold stayed right once fraud patterns shifted?
expected_points: 90% precision was set with product and fraud operations based on the cost of a false positive (manual review) versus the expected loss from a missed fraud.
Translated business costs into a precision/recall target instead of picking a round number.
Chose the threshold on a held-out time period's PR curve, then validated expected cost on a separate out-of-time window.
Set up scheduled or on-demand recalibration using recent labeled feedback and monitored live precision/recall.
When fraud mix shifted, reassessed the threshold with the same cost function rather than re-tuning to chase a metric.

question_hint: The resume says TimeSeriesSplit prevented leakage in a 40M-transaction dataset. What specific leakage were you protecting against, and why wasn't a plain TimeSeriesSplit enough?
expected_points: Random k-fold leaked future behavior into training, since fraud patterns and merchant or card attributes shift over time.
Beyond ordering splits by transaction timestamp, used a gap or embargo between train and validation to avoid overlapping label windows.
Grouped transactions by card or account so the same entity was not split across train and test.
Rejected features computed over the full dataset (e.g., global target encodings) and used time-aware aggregations from data strictly before the prediction timestamp.
Validated the model's uplift on champion-vs-challenger backtests across later time periods.

question_hint: You monitor feature drift with PSI > 0.2 and keep rollback under five minutes. Walk me through what happens when that alert fires—what do you check, and when do you actually roll back or retrain?
expected_points: The PSI alert triggers a runbook, not an automatic rollback; first investigate which features drifted and correlate with pipeline or product changes.
Compare current score distribution and business metrics (approval/decline rates, fraud rate) before acting, because feature drift can be benign or seasonal.
Roll back when score or fraud metrics degrade and a newer model version is suspect; a versioned registry and canary deployment enable fast reversion.
If drift is real but no metric regression yet, trigger retraining on recent labeled data and validate with time-aware offline evaluation before deploying.
Also monitor label drift or feedback delay, since PSI on features alone can miss a silent shift in the target.

question_hint: You cut inference p99 from 180 ms to 45 ms with a Redis feature store and batching. What was actually making p99 high, and what correctness or operational risks did batching introduce?
expected_points: Profiling showed most of p99 came from many sequential feature-lookup network round trips and serialization, not from XGBoost's predict call itself.
Moved high-cardinality reference features into Redis to eliminate per-request round trips and verified the gain with a canary before/after.
Batching trades single-request latency for throughput; used bounded batch windows and sizes so the p99 tail did not blow up, and load-tested under peak traffic.
Had to handle staleness and consistency between the Redis cache and source of truth, and define whether slight feature lag was acceptable for fraud decisions.
Added a fallback path for cache misses and monitored p99, error rate, and freshness during rollout.

question_hint: You reported 89% answer faithfulness using an LLM judge. How did you validate the judge itself, and how do you know that number reflects actual answer quality rather than judge bias?
expected_points: Built a small human-labeled set of grounded versus ungrounded answers and measured judge agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa or recall on hallucinated cases) before trusting it.
Tuned the judge prompt with clear definitions and few-shot examples, and checked for leniency on fluent but unsupported claims.
Separated retrieval quality from answer faithfulness, because a judge can appear accurate when the retriever already surfaced the right source.
Analyzed judge disagreements by failure mode and spot-checked a sample with human review to confirm the 89% estimate.

topic: Retrieval golden sets and CI regression gates
question_hint: You put Recall@5 for retrieval into CI regression gates. How stable was that metric on your golden set? Did a gate ever block a good change, and what did you do about it?
expected_points: The golden set needed enough queries and multiple judged relevant docs per query, otherwise Recall@5 variance made gates flaky.
Used a regression threshold compared with the baseline system on the same set, setting the margin from observed variance instead of a fixed global target.
Kept the golden set quarantined from training data and versioned it; refreshed it with new real queries while checking overlap.
When a gate blocked what looked like a good change, diffed the specific failures and either corrected noisy labels or supplemented Recall@5 with nDCG/MRR.
Treated CI gates as fast approximate safety checks and still required the full offline eval harness before production canary.

question_hint: The resume says you distilled an LLM labeler into a small classifier at 1/100th serving cost. How did you compare the student to the teacher, and how did you decide the quality loss was acceptable?
expected_points: Compared the student classifier against the teacher on held-out labels, and also validated F1 0.87 against human-labeled examples rather than only teacher agreement.
Measured downstream impact of routing errors (e.g., resolution time or handoff rate) to decide the quality loss was acceptable for the cost saving.
Quantified serving cost per prediction for both the LLM and the classifier in the actual deployment stack to justify the 1/100th figure.
Added a low-confidence fallback to the LLM so rare hard cases still got high-quality routing.
Set up a periodic distillation loop so the student stayed aligned as the teacher improved over time.

topic: Class imbalance treatment: class weights vs resampling
question_hint: On Meridian Pay, you wrote that you chose 'class weights over resampling after ablation.' Walk me through that ablation: what did you compare, on what data, and why did class weights win?
expected_points: Defined a shared, time-based validation split so resampling and class weights were compared on the same non-synthetic, out-of-time data.
Compared PR-AUC and cost-weighted metrics, not just ROC-AUC, because fraud is rare and errors have asymmetric costs.

Found resampling increased training variance or risk of overfitting (e.g., excessive duplicates, synthetic noise) and worsened calibration, while class weights achieved comparable or better precision-recall with less complexity.
Tested robustness across multiple temporal holdouts or business segments (e.g., card-present vs card-not-present, new vs existing merchants) to ensure the choice was not a single-split artifact.
Stated the final decision was tied to the operating threshold: the goal was maximizing recall at 90% precision, not just the training method chosen in isolation.

question_hint: You mentioned that TimeSeriesSplit was key to preventing leakage. What were the actual leakage risks in the transaction data, and how did you ensure every feature and label had no look-ahead?
expected_points: Identified temporal leakage sources: rolling aggregate features (e.g., average spend over past week) could accidentally include future transactions if computed over the whole dataset before splitting.

Managed label delay: fraud flags often become known weeks later, so labels are right-censored; used an appropriate gap between the feature time and the label window so validation labels would realistically exist at decision time.
Split by transaction timestamp, with a training/validation gap to avoid overlapping feature windows across splits.
Built offline feature computation to mirror the online serving path (same SQL or feature-store functions) to prevent train/serve skew.
Handled entity leakage for repeat cards or merchants: prevented the same entity from appearing in both train and validation through grouping or applying a transaction-level cap.

topic: Threshold tuning and business operating point
question_hint: You quote 'recall 0.62 at 90% precision, up from 0.41.' How did you arrive at 90% precision, and how did you verify the improvement was real and not an artifact of a convenient threshold?
expected_points: Defined the precision target through a cost analysis: precision translates to operational costs like review queue size and false declines, while recall maps to fraud dollars saved; the 90% figure was agreed with product/ops based on that economics.
Reported the 0.41 baseline at the same 90% precision point on the same temporal split, not simply a different PR-AUC, so the comparison at a fixed operating point was head-to-head.
Tuned the threshold on a validation fold, then confirmed on a separate out-of-time holdout to ensure the threshold generalized rather than overfitting to the validation curve.
Considered expected value per transaction (average fraud amount vs false-positive cost) and looked at the total cost curve, rather than plucking 90% arbitrarily.
Monitored the threshold as a live business parameter, so changing economics or risk appetite could be converted to a new threshold without retraining the model.

question_hint: You said you served the model behind FastAPI on Kubernetes with a canary rollout. How did you define a successful rollout? Walk me through the metrics and decisions that let you shift from 5% to 25% to 100% traffic.
expected_points: Started with shadow scoring or an offline replay so the candidate could be compared on live traffic without affecting decisions.
Selected a primary business metric with a pre-specified decision rule, e.g., fraud recall at a matched review rate, false-positive rate, decline rate, or adjusted revenue.
Used progressive traffic splits (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with automated guardrails: halt the canary if p99 latency, error rate, or any guardrail metric crossed a threshold.
Applied a statistical test or confidence interval with a target sample size, and accounted for seasonality by comparing canary traffic to simultaneous champion traffic, not to last week's baseline.
Tied the rollout to the versioned model registry, so rollback was a one-step alias switch and could be executed in minutes if the canary showed a metric regression.

topic: Feature drift monitoring and rollback playbook
question_hint: You mentioned 'feature drift monitoring pages on PSI > 0.2' and rollback via a versioned registry. When that alert fired, what was your playbook — did you retrain, roll back, or investigate first?
expected_points: Clarified the alert tracked per-feature PSI and prediction-score PSI on rolling windows; PSI > 0.2 was a configurable threshold chosen because normal seasonality occasionally pushed it to 0.15-0.2 without harm.
The first action was to investigate the cause: upstream feature source changes, data pipeline bugs, or genuine shifts in user/merchant behavior, rather than blindly retraining.
Because fraud labels are delayed, monitored credit-card fraud outcomes on recent traffic using a delayed-label framework, and only retrained if actual business performance degraded.
Retraining was scheduled but drift alerts triggered a performance investigation and, if metrics truly degraded, a rollback to a known-good registry version—expected done in under five minutes.
Had a clear distinction between feature drift (input distribution shift) and concept drift (changing relationship between features and label); the playbook handled each differently.

question_hint: You claim p99 inference time was cut from 180 ms to 45 ms by 'moving feature lookups to a Redis feature store and batching model calls.' How did you know those were the bottlenecks, and how did you keep features consistent with offline training?
expected_points: Profiled the request path: XGBoost scoring itself is often only a few milliseconds, so the p99 was likely dominated by repeated remote database calls for feature lookups rather than compute.
Identified that the p99 was driven by network round-trip latency and DB throttle, not by model size, so Redis with pipelining/MGET to fetch many features in one call removed the bottleneck.
Implemented a local cache or connection pooling on top of Redis to handle hot entities and reduce p99 variance further.

Designed 'batching' carefully: adaptive micro-batching or concurrent async calls improved throughput without violating per-request latency SLOs; could explain the tradeoff between delay and throughput.

Ensured train/serve consistency by deriving the Redis feature store from the same event stream or pipeline used to compute offline features, and audited sample transactions comparing store vs offline values.
Re-ran load tests under peak traffic and monitored p99 over several days to confirm the gain was stable, not just a cold-cache or low-traffic artifact.

question_hint: At Corvid, you report 'answer faithfulness measured with an LLM judge (89% grounded).' How was that judge built, and how did you validate that the 89% number reliably reflected true answer quality?
expected_points: Built a rubric-based LLM judge that checked whether the final answer was fully supported by the retrieved context, outputting a verdict and reasoning, not just a score.

Validated the judge against a set of human-annotated examples (e.g., 150-300 cases) and reported agreement metrics such as Cohen's kappa or judge precision/recall, making clear the 89% is on the golden set.

Mitigated known LLM-judge biases: varied the order of retrieved documents, sampled multiple judge runs, disabled chain-of-thought when only a verdict was needed, and watched for position or verbosity bias.

Compared against cheaper alternatives like NLI-based models or token-overlap metrics (ROUGE/BERTScore), ultimately choosing the LLM judge for its nuanced faithfulness detection but using it on a sampled set or offline harness only.
The 89% was used as a regression gate in CI, not as a standalone production metric; a drop below threshold triggered a review of retrieval quality or prompt changes before release.

topic: Offline evaluation harness and regression gates in CI
question_hint: You also mention building offline evaluation harnesses with golden sets, Recall@5 for retrieval, and regression gates in CI. What did a regression gate look like, and what made you trust it enough to block merges on it?
expected_points: Created a curated golden set of queries with relevant document labels, spanning intents and difficulty levels, separate from any training or prompt-development data.

Used Recall@5 as a retrieval health metric—was at least one relevant doc in the top five—chosen because it reflected whether the retriever surface area was sufficient for later reranking and generation.

Defined a regression as a statistically meaningful drop in Recall@5 on the golden set or a specific subset (e.g., high-urgency tickets) using a confidence interval or bootstrap instead of a single noisy number.
Set up the gate as a CI step that ran whenever retrieval config, embeddings, or reranker code changed, comparing against a frozen baseline with a tolerated margin to avoid flaky failures.
The thresholds were tuned on real failures the team had seen, and the harness itself was versioned and periodically refreshed with new failure cases to keep it relevant.

question_hint: Your Corvid bullet says you shipped 'BM25 + embedding hybrid retrieval over 12k internal docs.' Start there: exactly how did you run the two retrievers in parallel and combine their outputs, and what did you change after the first version?
expected_points: Rationale for hybrid: BM25 captures exact IDs, product names, and terminology while embeddings capture paraphrase and semantic matches; you compared each retriever alone before committing to hybrid.
Score fusion method: normalized BM25 and dense scores before a weighted sum or rank-based fusion, with weights tuned on a held-out query set.
Measured retrieval quality with Recall@5 or Recall@10 and end-to-end answer quality, not qualitative examples; hybrid beat either single retriever by a meaningful margin.
Handled latency by running the retrievers in parallel and capping the number of fused candidates before reranking.
Lesson learned: no single retriever was robust enough across 12k varied internal documents, and fusion only worked after calibrating the two score scales.

question_hint: You said retrieval covered 12k internal docs. How did you decide what a good unit of retrieval was — what did you do about chunk size, overlap, and document structure before you embedded them?
expected_points: Catalogued the actual doc sources and cleaned extraction artifacts or boilerplate before indexing.
Chose structure-aware chunks such as sections or headings instead of a single fixed size, and tested chunk size and overlap variants on retrieval metrics.
Attached metadata like source, section path, and timestamps to chunks so retrieval could filter or rerank on it.
Traded off chunk size: smaller chunks improved fidelity and Recall@5 but could starve the generator of context, so you picked a practical middle ground.
Evaluated chunking changes on retrieval and final-answer quality rather than intuition.

question_hint: Your bullet puts 'reranking' in the pipeline. What reranker did you use, why did you add reranking instead of just taking top-k from hybrid retrieval, and how did you prove it helped?
expected_points: Chose a cross-encoder-style reranker that scores query-document pairs jointly, capturing interactions that a bi-encoder cosine score misses.
Compared no-rerank against reranking and possibly different reranker models on a separate query set to avoid tuning on the golden set.
Reranking let the system retrieve wide and then send a smaller set of high-precision passages to the LLM within the prompt budget.
Measured both retrieval precision or Recall and final answer faithfulness; the improvement justified the added latency and serving cost.
Understood the operational tradeoff: reranker is another model to serve and can become a bottleneck or stale if not aligned with index updates.

question_hint: The resume says 'answer faithfulness measured with an LLM judge (89% grounded).' Walk me through how you built that judge, how you knew you could trust it, and what '89% grounded' actually allowed you to claim.
expected_points: Defined groundedness operationally: every factual claim in the answer needs support in the retrieved evidence; the judge prompt encoded that rubric, often judging claim by claim.
Validated the judge against a set of human-annotated examples using agreement metrics such as Cohen's kappa and iterated on the judge prompt until agreement was acceptable.
Used structured or deterministic output parsing and took basic precautions against position or verbosity bias in the judge.
Clarified that 89% grounded was measured offline on a held-out or golden question set, combining both retrieval and generation, so it could catch retriever misses as well as hallucination.
Acknowledged limitations: LLM judges can be lenient or miss unsupported reasoning, so a small human eval set stayed in the loop.

topic: Offline evaluation harness and regression gates
question_hint: You mention 'golden sets, Recall@5 for retrieval, regression gates in CI.' Who wrote the golden set, what did it contain, and what specifically made a PR fail the regression gate?
expected_points: Golden set came from real user queries or support tickets plus edge cases, with expert labels for relevant documents and acceptable answer spans; you split it to avoid tuning on the test set.
CI ran a representative subset quickly and the full golden set on schedule or on demand; gates blocked PRs that regressed Recall@5 or groundedness beyond a set tolerance.
Each eval layer measured a different risk: retrieval recall for finding evidence, rerank precision for prompt quality, LLM judge for grounded outputs, and format checks for downstream parsing.
Thresholds were set empirically from current system performance plus an allowed margin and were revisited as the system improved.
Lesson: treating prompts, retrievers, and indices like code with regression tests made fast iteration safe.

question_hint: Corvid bullet two: 'Fine-tuned a small classifier to route tickets (F1 0.87), distilled from an LLM labeler at 1/100th of the serving cost.' How did you generate labels, what student model did you use, and what did routing actually change for users?
expected_points: Used the LLM as an offline teacher: zero-shot or few-shot labeling of historical tickets, with confidence filtering or self-consistency so only reliable labels were used for training.
Student was a small, cheap model such as a fine-tuned encoder or embedding plus linear head; it served at roughly 1/100th of the teacher's cost.
The 0.87 F1 was measured on a held-out set not seen by the teacher or student during training; you compared downstream outcomes, not just classifier accuracy.
Routing decisions changed system behaviour: sending tickets to the right document collection or deciding when RAG was needed, which improved answer relevance and reduced latency.
Lesson: distillation is useful when serving cost and speed matter, but you need to monitor for label bias and drift of the student relative to the teacher.

question_hint: You credit 'grounded prompting' in the Corvid system. Pick one prompt iteration you actually shipped and walk me through what changed and how you measured it — not just vibes.
expected_points: An early prompt produced speculative or unsupported answers, so you added instructions to answer only from the provided evidence and to say explicitly when evidence was insufficient, possibly with few-shot examples of grounded versus ungrounded answers.
Evaluated both prompt versions on the exact same golden set and LLM judge, tracking groundedness or faithfulness before and after the change.
Kept prompts versioned and logged prompt metadata so a regression in production could be traced back to a specific change.
Understood that grounded prompting alone cannot fix a retrieval miss; you paired prompt changes with retrieval or reranking improvements.
Used measurable thresholds such as the final 89% grounded number to decide when the prompt was ready, rather than eyeballing sample outputs.

topic: Hybrid retrieval design and score fusion
question_hint: Ask: 'You said BM25 + embedding hybrid retrieval over 12k internal docs. Walk me through how you combined the two retrieval lists and what made you choose hybrid in the first place.'
expected_points: Explained why hybrid: BM25 is precise on exact terms/IDs/code but misses paraphrases and synonyms; embeddings capture semantic similarity but fail on rare tokens; hybrid is robust.
Described a concrete fusion method (e.g., Reciprocal Rank Fusion or weighted normalized-score sum), not a vague 'combined the lists'.
Mentioned alternatives considered and rejected: pure BM25 or pure embedding, with a measured retrieval metric (e.g., Recall@5) that showed hybrid was better.
Noted that the reranker came after fusion and absorbed ranking mismatches, so the fusion method did not need perfect score calibration.
Referred to real query/doc types (e.g., error codes, policy questions) that exposed the weakness of a single retriever.

question_hint: Ask: 'For the 12k internal docs, what chunking strategy did you use and how did you evaluate that it was the right call?'
expected_points: Described a concrete chunking setup: approximate token size (e.g., 200–500 tokens), overlap, and, crucially, that it respected document structure like headings or code blocks.
Mentioned that chunking was validated via the retrieval golden set or by the downstream LLM judge, not by intuition.
Explained how chunk metadata (source URL, doc title, section) was attached so the LLM could cite and identify context.
Discussed tradeoffs: smaller chunks increase precision but lose local context; larger chunks give context but exceed embedding/LLM windows or dilute relevance.
Gave an example of how a poorly considered chunking decision (e.g., splitting inside a numbered troubleshooting step) broke retrieval and how it was fixed.

question_hint: Ask: 'You listed reranking in the pipeline. Which reranker did you use and what happened to retrieval quality after you added it?'
expected_points: Named a reranker type or specific model (e.g., a cross-encoder, bge-reranker, or a lightweight scoring model), even if they used a hosted reranking API.
Quantified the effect: e.g., hybrid Recall@5 improved by a meaningful margin after reranking and/or final answer groundedness went up, measured on the same golden set.
Described the latency/cost tradeoff: rerank only top N candidates (e.g., 10–20) instead of all 50–100 to stay within p99 budget.
Mentioned that reranking was particularly valuable because fusion of BM25 and embedding lists had introduced irrelevant items near the top.
Clarified the position of reranking in the pipeline and how its output was fed into the grounded-prompt context.

topic: Validating the LLM judge for faithfulness
question_hint: Ask: 'You evaluated answer faithfulness with an LLM judge and reported 89% grounded. How did you verify that the judge itself was trustworthy?'
expected_points: Explained that they built a small human-annotated golden set of context/answer pairs and computed judge agreement with human labels (e.g., Cohen's kappa, accuracy).
Described iterating on the judge prompt: defining 'faithful', asking for textual support, using chain-of-thought or a rubric, and randomizing context order to control position bias.
Mentioned known LLM-as-judge failure modes: verbosity or length bias, favoring claims quoted directly from context, and how they mitigated or calibrated for them.
Set a confidence boundary: when judge confidence was low, they kept those examples for human review instead of trusting the judge blindly.
Explained that the judge was the main regression harness for faithfulness and was itself versioned and revalidated.

question_hint: Ask: 'The groundedness score was probably not 89% on the first try. Walk me through the measured iterations to your prompt and context assembly that moved it to that number.'
expected_points: Described an eval-driven loop: ran the offline harness, inspected failure examples, changed prompt/context, and re-ran to see if groundedness improved.
Gave at least one concrete failure pattern: the model answered from its own parametric memory even when context contradicted it, or it phrased an answer that wasn't supported.
Showed the fix: e.g., adding 'Only use the provided context. If the context is insufficient, say that and provide a support article link instead of guessing.'
Explained a context-formatting change: separating instructions from search-result blocks with clear delimiters, adding document titles and chunk IDs so the model could cite.
Acknowledged the tradeoff between strict grounding and usefulness—being too conservative can make answers unhelpful—and how they balanced it by measuring both faithfulness and failure/containment.

topic: Label generation and distillation for the ticket router
question_hint: Ask: 'The router classifier was fine-tuned from LLM labels and ran at 1/100th of the serving cost. How did you generate reliable labels and prove the distilled classifier was good enough to ship?'
expected_points: Described the label process: sampled historical tickets, sent them to an LLM with a strict routing taxonomy and few-shot examples, then used confidence thresholds and/or human agreement to only keep clean labels.

Reported how F1 0.87 was measured on a held-out set, and clarified that micro-F1 hides bad classes; they looked at per-class precision/recall because routing mistakes have different costs (e.g., urgent escalations missed).
Talked about the teacher-student gap: a subset where student and teacher disagreed was reviewed, then label definitions or the prompt were fixed, or noisy examples were dropped.
Gave real cost numbers: LLM teacher cost per thousand calls (e.g., $X) vs small-transformer CPU cost (e.g., $Y), and showed how 1/100th was calculated, including latency.
Explained how the router fit into the larger system, e.g., sending tickets to the RAG assistant, a human agent, or an escalation queue.

topic: Offline eval harness and CI regression gates
question_hint: Ask: 'You mention golden sets, Recall@5 for retrieval, and regression gates in CI. How did you build the golden set, and what stopped it from going stale over time?'
expected_points: Described creating the golden set from real user queries and known-resolved tickets, with multiple relevant docs per query; possibly augmented with synthetic variants.
Defined Recall@5 precisely (e.g., percentage of queries where at least one labeled relevant doc is in the top 5) and said why they also used MRR or precision.
Explained the CI gate: run the retrieval pipeline against a fixed index snapshot and fail the build if Recall@5 dropped by more than a small threshold (e.g., 3 points).
Mentioned that golden sets go stale and described a refresh process: periodically sample new production queries and relabel them, or use an LLM as a first-pass labeler with human review.
Gave a concrete example of a regression the gate caught: e.g., a change in fusion weights or embedding model silently degraded one query cohort.

topic: Production latency optimization and rollback habits
question_hint: Ask: 'On the Meridian Pay fraud service you cut inference p99 from 180ms to 45ms with a Redis feature store and batching. What tradeoffs did you make, and how does that experience shape the way you would optimize an LLM pipeline for latency and cost?'
expected_points: Explained that moving feature lookups to Redis removed a cross-service network hop and made features pre-materialized; model inference was not the original bottleneck.
Described batching tradeoffs: higher throughput and better GPU/API utilization vs an increase in latency tail from waiting for a full batch, so they tuned batch size/interval to hit p99 SLO.
Showed an ability to transfer the framework to LLM features: cache repeated LLM calls or embedding lookups, batch small requests where possible, and reconsider candidate count in retrieval.
Mentioned canary deploy, PSI drift monitoring, and fast rollback via a versioned model registry, and how that operational maturity applies to prompt/model versions in an LLM feature.
Highlighted the underlying principle: measure end-to-end before optimizing and keep rollback paths tested.

topic: Class imbalance: class weights vs resampling
question_hint: You wrote that you used XGBoost on 40M transactions with heavy class imbalance and chose class weights over resampling after an ablation. Walk me through exactly what you changed in that ablation, how you measured which option won, and why class weights were the right call for this problem.
expected_points: Compared class-weight XGBoost against alternatives like random under/oversampling or SMOTE, keeping the same features and base model.
Used the same time-based validation split (TimeSeriesSplit) for all candidates to make the comparison fair.
Selected based on PR curve behavior — e.g., recall at 90% precision or PR-AUC, not just ROC AUC.
Chose class weights because it was competitive or better on that metric without duplicating/synthesizing data or slowing training, and was simpler to ship.
Checked that results weren't an artifact of leakage — e.g., synthetic duplicates straddling train/test.

question_hint: You say you tuned a threshold on the PR curve to get recall 0.62 at 90% precision, up from 0.41. How did you decide 90% precision was the right cutoff, and what would you change if each false negative cost 100x a false positive?
expected_points: Explained that threshold is a business decision linking true/false positive rates to costs of manual review/decline vs fraud losses.
Described the baseline (0.41 recall) as the default 0.5 threshold or existing model, which was not the business optimum.
Used estimated cost per false positive (e.g., card decline friction, customer support) vs false negative (fraud amount) to pick the operating point.
If FN cost were 100x, they would move to a lower precision/higher recall point, roughly minimizing expected cost.
Mentioned they monitored live precision/recall after deployment since offline PR can overstate performance.

question_hint: You validated with TimeSeriesSplit to prevent leakage. Can you give a concrete example of the kind of leakage you were guarding against in your fraud features and labels, and how you structured the folds to avoid it?
expected_points: Identified time-dependent features like rolling card velocity or merchant statistics that would use future data if computed on the full history.
Noted label leakage — a fraud label may appear only after a dispute weeks later, so training must exclude windows where labels aren't yet known.
Structured split chronologically: earlier months train, later months validate, possibly with a gap to mimic live delay.
Mentioned no random shuffle and no single-row split because same-card or same-user transactions appear across splits.
Validated that both feature creation and labels use only past information at inference time.

topic: From offline metrics to real-world impact
question_hint: You reported recall 0.62 at 90% precision offline. How did you or your team measure whether the deployed model actually reduced fraud losses? And why can historical precision be misleading about live performance?
expected_points: Designed an online evaluation — canary/champion-challenger or A/B — rather than trusting the offline curve.
Tracked business metrics like fraud loss per approved transaction, false positive/decline rate, and review cost.
Noted distribution/concept drift and feedback loops: the model changes which orders are declined, altering the observed labels.
Explained offline historical labels are generated by old rules/systems, so live data contains new attack patterns.
Mentioned a specific guardrail example if they observed precision/recall degradation after rollout.

question_hint: You mentioned drift monitoring with PSI > 0.2 and rollback via a versioned registry. Imagine PSI crosses 0.2 tomorrow — what's the first thing you check before deciding to roll back vs retrain?
expected_points: First distinguishes data/feature drift from model performance drift — checks live labels if available and the model score distribution.
Investigates which features and segments drifted (new merchant category, seasonality) and whether the change is expected vs a system bug.
Checks whether an upstream data pipeline change caused a feature mapping bug rather than a real population shift.
Weighs the cost of the old model vs cost of retraining: if the drift is temporary or benign, no action may be needed.
Uses the versioned registry/canary to roll back quickly if performance is severely degraded, then retrains on new data.

question_hint: Your resume lists A/B testing under skills. Give me an example of an A/B test you designed end-to-end on one of your projects — specify the primary metric, unit of randomization, and sample size. How did you choose them?
expected_points: Selected a real or well-scoped hypothetical test around a model decision (e.g., threshold change or new model at the same operating point).
Chose a primary metric directly tied to business value, e.g., fraud loss per approved transaction, with guardrail metrics like approval rate, revenue, or support contacts.
Randomized at a unit where the treatment doesn't interfere — user/card level for fraud because transactions from the same user are correlated.
Pre-specified power and minimum detectable effect, used confidence intervals, and ran an AA test or checked invariant metrics.
If they didn't run a formal A/B test, acknowledged it and explained the alternative (canary with historical baseline) while being clear about causal limitations.

question_hint: You built offline evaluation harnesses for the RAG assistant: golden sets, Recall@5 for retrieval, regression gates in CI, and an LLM judge for groundedness. Of those, which number do you trust the most versus the least, and how did you keep the LLM judge from silently inflating the metric?
expected_points: Identified Recall@5 on a golden set can be inflated if the golden set is small, built from the same docs used in retrieval, or if queries overlap with training data.
Distinguished that the LLM judge's '89% grounded' number needs validation against human labels, and may be biased by answer length or wording.
Mentioned a held-out golden set created by independent humans, stratified by topic, not used during prompt development.
Described how they validated the judge itself — e.g., small human-labeled subset, measuring agreement, and inspecting failure modes.
Explained that regression gates in CI prevent overfitting to the eval set, but release decisions require fresh data or live traffic monitoring.

topic: Initial problem framing for the fraud model
question_hint: You built an XGBoost fraud model on 40M transactions with heavy class imbalance. How did you first frame the business problem, and how did you know a model was needed over the existing approach?
expected_points: Clearly articulate that the core question was 'which transactions are most likely to be fraudulent' and how that connects to revenue, user trust, and operational load
Describe the incumbent process (e.g., rule-based heuristics or a vendor score) and its shortcomings using evidence like missed fraud or false decline rates
Define success with business stakeholders before modeling: e.g., recall at a fixed precision to keep review-team workload acceptable
Show they quantified false positive and false negative costs and used that to weigh the model against the heuristic

question_hint: Your resume says you chose class weights over resampling after an ablation. Can you walk me through the ablation design and what led you to that decision?
expected_points: Name the methods compared (e.g., class weights, random undersampling/oversampling, SMOTE) and why resampling was considered at all
Specify the validation strategy: same TimeSeriesSplit folds and the same metric for all methods, not just accuracy or a single PR curve
Explain evidence: class weights gave the best recall at target precision (0.62 at 90% precision) with lower variance across time periods
Mention practical side benefits: no synthetic outliers, less training data duplication, simpler productionization, and robustness to shifts in fraud mix

topic: Threshold tuning and business tradeoffs on PR curves
question_hint: You tuned on PR curves to reach recall 0.62 at 90% precision, up from 0.41. What were the costs and benefits at that operating point, and how did you know 0.62 was the right number to ship?
expected_points: Construct a cost model: false positive cost (declined transaction, customer friction, manual review time) vs false negative cost (actual fraud loss, chargebacks)
Convert each PR-curve point into expected dollars and select the point minimizing expected loss, not just hitting a desired recall
Explain why 90% precision was chosen: perhaps operational capacity or a prior business constraint, and that it was revisited with the cost model

Translate the improvement from 0.41 to 0.62 recall at the same precision into business impact (e.g., catching ~50% more fraud without adding false positives, reduced annual fraud losses by a defensible amount)
Note they communicated the tradeoff to non-technical reviewers using a simple narrative or visual, not just PR curves

question_hint: You said you validated with TimeSeriesSplit to prevent leakage. What leakage were you really protecting against, and how did you implement the split so the model would hold up in production?
expected_points: Explain that fraud data is strongly temporal: a model trained on future transactions would have leaked information about merchant behavior and outcome labels
Random KFold would shuffle transactions from different months into train and test, letting test samples influence features or labels and causing overly optimistic PR curves

Describe using an expanding window or the standard TimeSeriesSplit, plus an embargo or purge window to prevent autocorrelation between adjacent time periods and avoid target leakage from rolling features
Admit that TimeSeriesSplit alone does not stop concept drift and that they paired it with periodic retraining and monitoring in production

topic: Changing a real decision with the model
question_hint: In a senior DS role we care whether analysis changes decisions. What was Meridian Pay's fraud decision process before this model, and how did you actually change what the team did?
expected_points: Identify the prior process (e.g., rules-based alerting, third-party score, or manual review queues) and its false positive / missed fraud rate
Describe running a backtest on historical transactions to compare the XGBoost model and the incumbent on monetary terms, not just PR metrics
Mention using a shadow-mode or canary rollout where model scores were logged but decisions stayed unchanged, and then measuring what would have been caught/changed
Show they presented results in business language (fraud dollars saved, false declines reduced, review volume needed) to gain buy-in from payments risk, product, and engineering stakeholders
State the eventual outcome: e.g., the model was integrated into the real-time transaction decisioning or review queue, which is a clear decision change

topic: Monitoring with PSI and rollback thresholds
question_hint: You built feature drift monitoring with PSI > 0.2 and rollback in under five minutes. How did you pick 0.2 as the alert threshold, and when do you think PSI could give false confidence on the model's health?
expected_points: Acknowledge that PSI > 0.2 is a standard industry rule of thumb based on historical experience, and that they calibrated it against a baseline period to avoid alert fatigue
Distinguish feature drift from target or concept drift: stable features do not guarantee stable model performance, especially if fraud patterns shift unexpectedly
Give an example: criminal behavior changes (e.g., new merchant category or card testing strategy) while aggregate feature distributions stay similar, so detection quality silently drops
Mention they also tracked online business metrics (e.g., fraud rate among flagged transactions, false positive rate) alongside PSI, and that alerts triggered a canary review and rollback path
Explain that rollback requires a versioned registry and model comparison, and they practiced it to make the 5-minute rollback realistic

topic: Evaluating faithfulness with an LLM judge
question_hint: For the support assistant you said answer faithfulness was measured with an LLM judge at 89% grounded. How did you validate the judge, and where do you think LLM judges can be systematically wrong?
expected_points: Built a golden set with human-annotated groundedness and compared judge labels to human labels, measuring agreement, precision, and recall of the judge itself
Calibrated the judge prompt with few-shot examples and adjusted thresholds after seeing failure cases
List known failure modes: judge may be lenient on style/length, miss subtle hallucinations, or be biased toward answers that mimic the reference
Explain that when the judge disagreed with humans, they did spot checks, reviewed adversarial cases, and periodically refreshed the golden set
Mention they did not rely solely on the 89% number; they also monitored groundedness against human-rewritten goldens and had a human review process for low-confidence answers

topic: Distillation from LLM labels for ticket routing
question_hint: You fine-tuned a classifier from LLM labels and achieved F1 0.87 at 1/100th the cost. How did you make sure the LLM teacher labels were good enough, and what was the real accuracy/efficiency tradeoff you accepted?
expected_points: Created LLM labels with a high-quality prompt, then human-validated a representative subset; measured teacher agreement and only used labels from high-confidence or self-consistent teacher responses
Evaluated the student on a human-labeled held-out set, not on teacher labels, to avoid inheriting the teacher's blind spots
Shared the tradeoff explicitly: e.g., small F1 drop vs ~100x latency/cost reduction was acceptable for routing use case, and they verified cost savings against the LLM call expense
Described iterative clean-up: when the teacher was wrong, they added adversarial examples or corrected labels, not just blindly trained on LLM output
Mentioned they considered an alternative (running LLM directly for routing) and rejected it because of cost and latency constraints, not just because of F1

topic: Latency optimization via Redis feature store and batching
question_hint: You mention cutting p99 from 180 ms to 45 ms by moving feature lookups to a Redis feature store and batching model calls. What did the latency breakdown look like, and why did those two changes produce that drop?
expected_points: Profiled request latencies and identified that per-request feature lookups dominated, not the XGBoost inference itself.
Moved hot features into Redis, designing the key schema and population/invalidation strategy to keep data fresh while avoiding costly upstream calls.
Added batching to amortize per-call overhead and measured how batch size trades off p99 latency against throughput.
Ran load tests with representative traffic before and after each change to isolate the 180 ms to 45 ms improvement.
Handled cache misses and fallback to the source store so Redis availability was not a single point of failure.

topic: Canary rollout and versioned model registry rollback
question_hint: You say you served the model behind FastAPI on Kubernetes with canary rollout, and rollback via versioned model registry in under five minutes. What does that pipeline actually look like—how do you decide a canary is safe, and how do you execute the rollback?
expected_points: Model artifact is versioned in a registry; deployment points to a specific version and the Kubernetes manifests are reproducible via GitOps.
Canary starts by routing a small percentage of live traffic to the new model, while the rest goes to the stable version.
During canary they compare error rates, latency, and a business proxy metric (e.g., decline rate or review rate) because true fraud labels are delayed.
A rollback is shifting traffic back to the previous model version from the registry, and they validated in a game day that it completes in under five minutes.
They also defined a clear go/no-go decision criteria for promoting a canary to 100% traffic.

question_hint: You set up feature drift monitoring with PSI and a threshold of 0.2. What is PSI measuring in that context, and when the alarm goes over 0.2, what do you actually do?
expected_points: Explains PSI as a measure of distribution shift between a reference window and the current window for key input features.
Monitors not just raw features but also the model's predicted score distribution, and knows a PSI above 0.2 is an alert, not necessarily a reason to roll back.
On alert they investigate whether the change is legitimate (e.g., new customer segment, seasonality, upstream system change) or a broken feature pipeline.
They correlate drift with actual model performance when labels arrive to avoid noisy alarms leading to action.
Built a drift dashboard with a list of drifting features and trends so an on-call engineer can quickly triage.

topic: Class imbalance handling and PR threshold tuning
question_hint: You said you chose class weights over resampling after ablation and tuned the threshold on PR curves to get recall 0.62 at 90% precision. What did the ablation practically test, and how did you decide that operating point was right for the business?
expected_points: Ran offline experiments comparing random oversampling, SMOTE, and class weights, using TimeSeriesSplit; chose class weights because it matched or beat resampling and was simpler to productionize.
Understood that both resampling and class weights shift the score distribution, so the final decision boundary is a separate threshold chosen on the PR curve.
Business context: fraud review costs and false positive impact set a target of around 90% precision; at that precision the model got recall 0.62 vs a baseline 0.41.
Also considered monetary loss: a false negative has a dollar loss that varies by transaction size, so the threshold could be weighted by amount rather than just by count.
Threshold tuning was validated on out-of-time data to avoid selecting a threshold that only works on the training period.

question_hint: You mentioned validating with TimeSeriesSplit to prevent leakage. Tell me about a specific leakage trap this caught, and how you structured the splits for 40M transactions.
expected_points: Random splitting transaction data leaks because the same user's historical transactions end up in both train and test, and rolling features can incorporate future information.
Structured splits by time, training on earlier months and evaluating on later ones, and included an embargo or gap to account for delayed fraud labels.
Caught a concrete example where a rolling feature computed over the entire transaction history was using transaction timestamps beyond the scoring cutoff, inflating offline PR/AUC.
The fix was to strictly limit feature computation to information available at the exact transaction timestamp (only past transactions, not future ones).
Understood that TimeSeriesSplit gives a more honest estimate of online performance, and they used it to decide between class weights and resampling as well.

topic: Offline evaluation harness and CI regression gates
question_hint: You mention building offline evaluation harnesses with golden sets and Recall@5 as regression gates in CI. What did the harness check, and what's a regression it caught?
expected_points: The harness used a golden set of queries with manually or LLM-labeled relevant documents, and computed retrieval metrics like Recall@5 and MRR.
It ran automatically in CI whenever retrieval code, embeddings, or ranking logic changed, failing the build if a metric dropped below a defined threshold.
Caught a real regression when switching to a new embedding model shifted the vector space and degraded hybrid retrieval results for a segment of queries.
The CI gate gave fast feedback and reduced the cost of deploying a silent search-quality regression.
Learned that golden sets need to be versioned and refreshed periodically to cover new question types or document updates.

topic: Distilled classifier and serving cost measurement
question_hint: You say you fine-tuned a small classifier distilled from an LLM labeler at 1/100th of the serving cost. How did you design the distillation and how did you measure that cost saving without sacrificing quality?
expected_points: Used the LLM as a noisy labeler to generate training data or soft labels, then trained a small classifier on the resulting dataset.
Evaluated the small model on a held-out test set and measured F1 0.87; compared it against the LLM labeler's F1 on the same test set to ensure parity within business tolerance.
Cost was measured as a per-inference figure including compute infrastructure (e.g., GPU vs CPU), serving overhead, and scaling costs—not just raw model latency.
Set up a fallback strategy where low-confidence predictions from the small model went to the LLM, which bounded the downside of the cheaper model.
Monitored production metrics over time to ensure the performance held up as the ticket distribution drifted.

topic: FastAPI/Kubernetes serving architecture and latency optimization
question_hint: You called out serving the model behind FastAPI on Kubernetes and getting p99 from 180ms to 45ms. Walk me through the request path before and after—where was the 180ms going, and what did you change besides batching?
expected_points: Describes original request path: per-request feature lookups from source data, one model call per request, and any upstream/downstream service calls.
Identifies the dominant p99 bottleneck through profiling/load testing—likely repeated expensive feature aggregation or serial model inference.
Explains the changes: precomputed features in Redis, batched model calls (e.g., collecting a window of scoring requests), async FastAPI handling, and tuning resource requests/limits or HPA for K8s.
States how p99/latency was verified (load test, shadow traffic, production monitoring) without regressing accuracy or other metrics.
Discusses horizontal scaling tradeoffs: pod count, concurrency, downstream Redis/model server saturation, and cost impact.

topic: Redis feature store design and consistency
question_hint: You mentioned moving feature lookups to a Redis feature store. What exactly is stored—raw features or computed features—and how did you handle consistency (missing values, delayed transactions, feature backfill) when you first launched?
expected_points: Clarifies feature store content: precomputed features (rolling transaction aggregates, merchant/user profiles) rather than raw transaction logs; keyed for low-latency MGET lookups.
Explains offline pipeline that computes features and writes to Redis, plus TTL/eviction strategy to keep memory bounded.
Describes fallback behavior on cache miss or Redis outage: recompute from a secondary store with degraded latency, or serve with default/neutral features while logging misses.
Details backfill for rollout: run historical feature computation against training data, verify coverage and distributions, then shadow traffic before enabling live traffic.
Covers staleness and delay: how late or duplicate events were handled, plus alerting on feature freshness and consistency checks.

topic: Canary rollout and model registry rollback
question_hint: You call out rollback via a versioned model registry in under five minutes. Walk me through what happens during a release and a rollback: what triggers it, who does it, and what makes it under five minutes rather than an hour?
expected_points: Describes model registry as source of truth: immutable artifacts with metadata (training window, feature schema, eval metrics, deployment history), used to reference any prior version at runtime.

Explains canary process: deploy new model as a separate deployment or traffic-split; start at low percentage and ramp based on metrics like p99, error rate, business metrics (fraud recall/false positives), and drift PSI.
States concrete rollback criteria: PSI > 0.2, p99/error-rate SLO violation, or precision drop; alert goes to on-call engineer with dashboard link.

Identifies why rollback is fast: a generic serving container pulls the model artifact from the registry at startup; rollback is a traffic/selector switch via Helm/kubectl to the previous version, no image rebuild or code deploy; verified through game days.
Discusses measured rollback time vs target and any incidents where rollback was actually exercised.

topic: Feature drift monitoring and alerting thresholds
question_hint: You set up drift monitoring pages alerting on PSI > 0.2. How do you compute PSI, what time windows do you compare, and why 0.2? What does an engineer do when the page goes red?
expected_points: Explains PSI computation: bucket each feature into bins, compare recent production distribution (hourly/daily samples from serving logs or Redis) to a training/reference distribution, sum (actual % - expected %) * ln(actual % / expected %).
Details monitoring infrastructure: scheduled job (Airflow or cron) reads feature values, computes PSI per feature, writes to time-series DB, visualizes in Grafana, and sends alerts to on-call.
Rationale for threshold: 0.2 is a standard PSI threshold; it was calibrated against past false positives and false negatives; it signals 'investigate', not necessarily 'rollback immediately'.

Describes incident response: check whether shift is expected (e.g., seasonality, new product), compare with model score distribution and fraud outcomes, inspect upstream feature pipelines for bugs; if the shift is real and persistent, retrain or rollback.
Mentioned aggregating alerts by feature importance to avoid paging on noisy low-impact features.

topic: Training pipeline scalability and reproducibility on 40M transactions
question_hint: Training on 40M transactions and serving it in production is one thing, but from a platform perspective, how did you organize the data pipeline and the training job? If I gave you a new date range, how would you regenerate the dataset and train the exact same model?
expected_points: Describes data pipeline: extract transaction data from warehouse, run feature generation jobs (SQL/Spark or Python) to create labeled feature snapshots stored in S3; schedule with Airflow; track versioned datasets.

Explains training job reproducibility: training code in git, Docker container with pinned dependencies, config file for XGBoost hyperparameters/class weights, data snapshot hash and code commit recorded; run in SageMaker or equivalent.

Addresses scale: 40M rows cannot fit naively in memory; describes partitioning, reading from S3 in chunks, or using distributed data processing (e.g., SageMaker/Spark) with CPU/memory limits and checkpointing.
Cites TimeSeriesSplit to prevent temporal leakage and explains why calendar-order splits are necessary in fraud detection.
Demonstrates ability to replay: re-running the same pipeline with recorded data version and code hash yields identical model artifact and evaluation metrics; a new date range just changes the config.

topic: Model evaluation, class imbalance, and leakage prevention
question_hint: You wrote that you used class weights over resampling after ablation and tuned thresholds on PR curves. As the person inheriting this model, what do I need to know about your evaluation setup and how you avoided leakage?
expected_points: Describes controlled ablation: same pipeline and evaluation methodology for class weighting vs SMOTE/undersampling; decision metric was PR AUC / recall-at-precision, leading to class weights for stability and lower training cost.
Details TimeSeriesSplit: training/validation splits respect transaction time, with a gap if needed; no random shuffling, and any feature derived from the future is explicitly excluded.

Explains label leakage pitfalls in fraud: labels arrive after delay (e.g., chargebacks); training features must use only information known at transaction time, and evaluation must reflect label-delay windows.

Describes threshold selection: set precision floor at 90% (business/friction constraint) and choose a threshold maximizing recall; recall improved from 0.41 to 0.62 at that precision on the validation PR curve.
Cautions about offline-to-online gap: PR gains don't automatically translate; validation used a final hold-out time period and online shadowing before canary.

topic: Offline evaluation harness and CI regression gates
question_hint: You mention building offline evaluation harnesses and regression gates in CI for the support assistant. Walk me through how that worked under CI—where did data and models come from, how long did it take, and how did a developer react when the gate failed?
expected_points: Defines the golden set: versioned, immutable set of queries/documents/expected outputs with known labels, stored in S3 or a data store; used for computing retrieval Recall@5, LLM-judge faithfulness, and routing classifier F1.

Describes CI integration: a GitHub Actions/GitLab pipeline runs on PRs touching model code; it spins up a container, downloads the golden set and model artifacts, runs evaluation, and posts metrics to the PR.

Explains regression gate criteria: metrics compared to a pinned baseline (e.g., main branch or latest model registry entry); PR fails if Recall@5 drops by more than a tolerance (e.g., 1 point) or if faithfulness score degrades.

Discusses runtime tradeoffs: running full evaluation on every PR is too slow/expensive, so used a small subset for CI and full nightly evaluation; used caching and model/dependency pinning to keep runs fast and deterministic.

Shares operational lesson: the gate sometimes blocked legit changes due to golden-set staleness or nondeterministic LLM judge; they added threshold tolerance and a review/override path, making the gate trustable.

topic: Distilled classifier and serving cost reduction
question_hint: You distilled the LLM labeler into a small classifier at '1/100th of serving cost.' How was that cost measured, and what evidence would convince me to trust that number and adopt this pattern across other use cases?
expected_points: Clarifies cost metric: cost per prediction (or per 1M predictions) including compute/API unit price and serving infrastructure (e.g., CPU instance vs GPU/LLM endpoint), measured under production-like load.

Describes distillation process: LLM generated labels on unlabeled tickets; low-confidence labels were filtered; small classifier (e.g., fine-tuned encoder) was trained to imitate the teacher; achieved F1 0.87 on the routing task.
Quantifies the tradeoff: small classifier is cheaper and faster but weaker on edge cases; they added confidence thresholds to fall back to LLM or human for low-confidence predictions.
Provides evaluation evidence: offline golden-set comparison showed no significant drop in business metrics (e.g., routing accuracy, downstream resolution), and online A/B or shadowing confirmed it.
Discusses maintenance: the teacher LLM and golden labels are revisited periodically to regenerate training data for the student, avoiding silent degradation from label/topic drift.

question_hint: Your resume says you picked 'XGBoost with class weights over resampling after ablation' on 40M transactions. Talk me through that ablation: what variants did you actually run, how did you keep the comparison fair, and why did class weights win for this problem?
expected_points: Compared class weighting against at least undersampling and oversampling (e.g., SMOTE), and likely an unweighted baseline, on the exact same train/validation folds.
Kept features, XGBoost hyperparameters, and evaluation protocol fixed so the only difference was the imbalance-handling technique.
Selected the operating threshold per technique on the PR curve rather than defaulting to 0.5, and compared recall at the target 90% precision.
Class weights won on PR trade-off, retained all transaction data, avoided synthetic-sample artifacts or variance from random undersampling, and was cheaper to retrain.
Also checked that class weights did not overfit the minority class by validating on a time-based holdout.

question_hint: You list recall at 90% precision going from 0.41 to 0.62. What was the model that produced that 0.41 baseline, and what business trade-off did you encode when you chose to report the metric at exactly 90% precision?
expected_points: Clarified the 0.41 baseline was the incumbent production model (or an earlier XGBoost without the redesigned feature pipeline) under the same fraud-operations definition.
Explained the operating point was set with the fraud-ops team: 90% precision was the minimum to avoid overwhelming manual reviews, so the model was thresholded to maximize recall at that precision.
The 0.41->0.62 recall gain means the new model caught ~21 more of every 100 true fraud transactions for the same false-positive budget.
Compared to the old thresholding policy (e.g., scoring threshold rather than explicit PR target) to show why precision/recall curve tuning was more honest.

question_hint: You say the fraud model was validated with TimeSeriesSplit to prevent leakage on 40M transactions. Give me a real leakage risk you had to engineer around, and how the time-based split changed your decisions.
expected_points: Mentioned transactions are sorted by timestamp and that random K-fold shuffling would let future transactions leak into training, inflating performance.

Described a concrete leakage trap: for example a rolling feature window that included the current transaction's outcome, or an unscored batch used at training while future labels were available; fixed by strictly ending features before transaction time.
TimeSeriesSplit accounted for covariate shift after product launches or policy changes; the model was revalidated on the most recent fold that matched production conditions.
Feature engineering had to use only lagged values, and any imputation could not use global future statistics; verified by detecting zero or near-zero gap on the earliest time windows.

question_hint: Your resume says the RAG assistant's answers were measured with an LLM judge and were '89% grounded'. Before trusting that number, how did you validate the judge, and what would you accept as evidence that the judge was wrong?
expected_points: Built a human-annotated evaluation set of assistant answers and measured judge-human agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa) rather than only relying on the LLM's self-report.
Tuned the judge prompt with few-shot grounded/ungrounded examples and required citations to retrieved chunks so it couldn't rely on parametric memory.
Stress-tested the judge on adversarial cases: partially grounded answers, plausible-sounding but wrong chunks, or answers correct but unsupported by retrieval.

Believed the 89% only to the extent it matched human review and canary outcomes; a random audit or low-confidence judge samples could falsify it if groundedness was much lower in cases that mattered to users.

question_hint: You built hybrid BM25 + embedding retrieval and then reranking over 12k docs. What baseline did you compare it against, and what evidence told you the hybrid stage and the reranker were each worth their added complexity?
expected_points: Established baselines: BM25-only and embedding-only (or dense-only) with the same reranker, measured on a golden set with Recall@5 and answer groundedness.

Hybrid fusion (with weights) improved recall over each single retriever, especially for queries with exact identifiers and natural-language phrasing; showed gains were material (e.g., +10-15% Recall@5).

Ablated the reranker: without it, adding hybrid improved retrieval but not end-to-end answer groundedness as much; with reranker the top-1 relevant doc was consistently first and groundedness improved.
Measured latency/budget per query: hybrid and reranker still fit the support experience's time limit; in cases where they didn't, BM25-only fallback or top-k truncation was in place.
Considered retrieval 'headroom' and counterfactual failure modes: pure embedding lost exact code/SKU matches, pure BM25 lost paraphrases.

topic: Distilled ticket classifier — F1 and cost
question_hint: You fine-tuned a classifier to F1 0.87 with labels distilled from an LLM at 1/100th the serving cost. What was the ground truth for that F1, and where was the acceptable quality/cost boundary for the ticket-routing use case?
expected_points: The F1 was measured on a held-out set of human-labeled tickets (not on LLM teacher labels), so it represented true routing quality after distillation.
Estimated teacher accuracy by sampling and human review of high-confidence and low-confidence LLM labels, then set aside a clean gold set for final student evaluation.

At 0.87 F1, the routing quality was comparable to the previous rule-based router or slightly better while reducing manual sort error; navigation/maybe user impact assessed by escalation/fallback rates.
Cost boundary: the student runs on CPU at 1/100 cost (e.g., a few ms vs hundreds of ms); even a few F1 points would be worth 100x cost only if those errors caused support failures.
Mentioned that they looked at per-class precision/recall, and used a fallback to human or LLM for low-confidence routing.

question_hint: You cut p99 inference from 180 ms to 45 ms by moving feature lookups to Redis and batching model calls. How did you verify that the 45 ms path returned predictions that were still correct given the feature store and batching changes?
expected_points: Ran offline regression: sampled production traffic, scored the old and new feature paths on the same requests, and confirmed the model outputs were identical or negligible differences in scores/predictions.
Verified Redis feature store parity with the source database (same keys, same up-to-second freshness, same missing/NaN semantics) to avoid changing model inputs silently.
Batching preserved per-request features by mapping responses back to request IDs; concurrency behavior was load-tested to ensure p99 improvement wasn't just queueing games.
Used canary/shadow deployment: served live traffic with the new path and compared prediction drift and business outcome over days before full rollout.
Would have rolled back if PSI on any feature exceeded 0.2 or if core fraud metrics moved by >X%.

topic: PSI drift monitoring threshold and blind spots
question_hint: You use PSI > 0.2 as your feature-drift alert in production. Why 0.2 specifically, and can you describe a real drift scenario that this PSI policy would miss?
expected_points: PSI 0.2 is a common rule-of-thumb threshold signifying a 'significant' distribution shift, and they calibrated it against historical stable periods to avoid alert fatigue.
PSI is univariate: it checks one feature's distribution at a time and can't capture multivariate or interaction drift even if model performance is degrading.

A blind spot: the feature distribution stays the same (e.g., transaction amount, merchant category) but the relationship between features and the fraud label changes (new fraud ring), causing recall/precision to drop while PSI stays < 0.2.
Also when a feature is highly skewed or binned coarsely, large raw shifts may not move PSI past 0.2, and vice versa.
Because of these limits, they paired PSI with target drift monitoring (actual vs expected fraud rate), performance monitoring, and rollback drills.

question_hint: The resume says you chose class weights over resampling after an ablation. Paint that picture for me — what exactly did you hold fixed, what variants did you compare, and which metric told you class weights were the right call?
expected_points: Held the feature set and base XGBoost hyperparameters constant; compared no handling, class weights, undersampling, oversampling/SMOTE, then did a small sweep on the class-weight ratio.
Used a business-oriented metric — such as PR AUC and recall at 90% precision — on each TimeSeriesSplit validation fold, not just log loss or global AUC.
Found resampling did not improve precision at the target recall and made performance less stable across folds; class weights produced a better precision-recall operating region.
Tuned the classification threshold separately on the PR curve after model training, so the reported recall at 90% precision reflects an operating point chosen from the business context.
Explained why precision at a fixed recall was preferred over raw F1 or AUC: false positives on valid transactions carry a concrete cost.

topic: Baseline and attribution of reported lift
question_hint: Your resume reports recall improving from 0.41 to 0.62 at 90% precision. What exactly was the 0.41 baseline, and what set of changes — in order — produced the lift?
expected_points: States precisely what the 0.41 baseline was: either the previous production model or a default XGBoost with no class weighting and default threshold, evaluated out-of-time on the same test period at 90% precision.
Decomposes the gain: class weights shifted the precision-recall tradeoff, and then threshold calibration moved along the curve to the 90% precision operating point.
Specifies the evaluation window: transactions after the training cutoff with at least N weeks of label delay to ensure fraud labels are reliable.
Explains why 90% precision was the target (cost of false positives drives review workload) and notes whether the gain held at other precision points, e.g., 80% or 95%.
Acknowledges sampling variance and reports that the gain was stable across time-based folds rather than a single lucky test set.

question_hint: You mentioned validating with TimeSeriesSplit to prevent leakage. Walk me through the most concrete leakage path you were guarding against in a 40M-transaction dataset — and how you made sure feature engineering was also leak-free.
expected_points: Explains that a random split would put the same card, account, or merchant in both train and test, letting the model memorize entity-level behavior that would not generalize to new fraud patterns.
Notes the feature-leakage pitfall: rolling aggregates computed over the whole 40M dataset or using the transaction's own future outcomes in a feature would leak future information into training.
Describes the validation design: expanding/rolling time windows with no shuffling and an enforced gap between train and validation to mimic delay between transaction time and confirmed fraud labels.
Mentions that labels themselves are time-aware: transactions at the end of the training period may not yet have a confirmed fraud label, so using them as negatives would bias the model.
Ensured point-in-time correctness: every feature value was computed only from data available at the transaction timestamp, both in training and in the serving feature store.

question_hint: You set a feature-drift alert at PSI > 0.2, with rollback via a versioned model registry in under five minutes. How did you choose 0.2 rather than adopting it as a convention, and what distinguishes a rollback from a retrain decision when the alarm fires?
expected_points: Explains that 0.2 sits at the conventional 'large shift' boundary but was validated empirically using historical drift episodes where model quality actually degraded.
Tracks PSI on the model score and a handful of top-importance input features, not on every feature, to avoid alert noise from unimportant drift.

Defines a clear decision path: if drift appears on core features alongside score drift, roll back the challenger immediately if canary guardrails are also failing; otherwise investigate and decide between a feature fix and a retrain.
Notes that the versioned model registry plus automated deployment made rollback a one-click action that was drilled and measured to be under five minutes.
Mentions that after rollback the team does root-cause analysis and revisits the PSI threshold when the drift/performance relationship becomes better understood.

question_hint: Tell me how the canary rollout for this fraud model actually worked. Which slice of traffic got the new model first, what did you compare it against, and what would have made you abort the rollout?
expected_points: Started with a small slice of low-exposure traffic, such as 5% of transactions below a value threshold or on a specific channel, to contain financial risk while still reaching statistical significance.
Ran champion versus challenger side-by-side on both real-time metrics (error rate, latency, decline/dispute rate) and delayed-label metrics like confirmed fraud recall once chargebacks arrived.
Set pre-agreed abort guardrails before launch, e.g., error rate above 1%, p99 latency over 100 ms, decline rate increase beyond a business threshold, or PSI above 0.2 on critical features.
Ramped traffic in stages (e.g., 5% -> 20% -> 50%) only when the guardrails were stable; the versioned registry allowed immediate rollback at any stage.
Chose canary complexity deliberately because for fraud a silent failure on 100% of traffic is far more expensive than a slower deployment.

topic: Latency optimization via Redis and batching
question_hint: You mention cutting inference p99 from 180 ms to 45 ms by moving feature lookups to Redis and batching model calls. Which features were problematic, and how did you prevent the optimization from changing what the model sees at serving time versus training time?
expected_points: Identified online features, like rolling transaction counts or amounts per card/merchant, as the high-latency lookups, while less mutable identity/merchant features could stay in batch tables.
Used a versioned Redis feature store with point-in-time correctness so the exact feature values available at request time were the same as those used during training, avoiding training-serving skew.
Explains batching did not change feature semantics; requests were grouped to improve throughput, with a bounded batch window and fallback to synchronous single-request mode to cap latency.
Measured not only p99 but also p50/p95 and timeout/error rates after the change to confirm the tail improvement was real and did not come from dropped or degraded requests.
Verified the model output was deterministic on the cached feature snapshot for a given request, so faster serving did not silently change the scoring decision.

question_hint: In the RAG support assistant you measured 'answer faithfulness' with an LLM judge and reported 89% grounded. How did you know the judge itself wasn't just giving you comfortable numbers — did you validate it against human annotations? And once you trusted the metric, was the bottleneck the retriever or the generator?
expected_points: Built a small human-labeled set of answers scored grounded/not grounded, ran the LLM judge on that set, and computed agreement such as percent agreement or Cohen's kappa, iterating on the judge prompt until disagreements were understood.
Judged the final answer against the retrieved passages rather than in isolation, with a rubric that penalized both hallucination and unsupported inference.
Also tracked retrieval Recall@5 / MRR and end-to-end faithfulness; found the hybrid BM25+dense retriever improved over either method alone, especially on exact terms versus paraphrases.

Performed error analysis that separated retriever failures (gold passage not in the top-k) from generator failures (passage present but answer not grounded); the fix differed — reranker/query expansion vs. grounding constraints/prompts.

Reported that the 89% number came from a fixed golden set with a realistic sample size, and compared against a non-grounded baseline to demonstrate the gain, rather than quoting a single number with no context.

topic: Distillation of LLM labeler into small classifier
question_hint: Your resume says the ticket router was a small classifier distilled from an LLM labeler at 1/100th of the serving cost, with F1 0.87. How did you generate trustworthy silver labels, and how did you prove the student model didn't just inherit the teacher's blind spots?
expected_points: Generated silver labels from the LLM on a stratified sample of historical tickets — including edge cases and multi-intent examples — using low-temperature sampling and a self-consistency/majority-vote step; discarded low-confidence or ambiguous labels.
Evaluated the distilled model on a separate, human-labeled gold set rather than on teacher-generated labels, so the F1 0.87 is an honest measure of student quality.
Compared the student against the pre-existing routing baseline (rules or larger model) at the relevant operating precision/recall, not just F1 in isolation.
Analyzed failure slices where the teacher was known to be weak (e.g., novel ticket types, conflicting intents) and added targeted human labels for those slices to prevent silent bias propagation.
Clarified the cost comparison: 1/100th refers to per-request serving cost/inference of the small classifier versus calling the LLM; one-time distillation/labeling cost was excluded but acknowledged.
